nodes.title: Round 7 (main's hybrid-pilot judgement, defects 8 and 9): code invariants on the agent lane's line (server/agent/invariants.js). From class 4 up: no counting-on or finger counting, no bare single-digit sum of her own, and at most 2 agent turns in a row in practice without a kit card. At most one engaged off-lesson turn in a row, and never a line that sets the lesson aside (maths abhi side mein). A line that breaks one is not sent: the Director's move and line take that turn and the runs restart. An agent end the Director did not make is the same (judgement #3).

Round 7 (judgement defect 10): a yes (haan, ok, theek hai) to the ways-in choices she just offered is answered by asking which one, with the same chips, never by dropping the offer. Naming one, or the chip, is its request as before.

Round 7 (judgement defect 11): with no game on the screen (no play piece, no mounted activity), a game never acts in her line (game ne, the game counted). The spoken-game shape says it is a game between the two of them, and a line that has a game act is caught (gameclaim): rewritten, or the sentence dropped.

md.decisions:
## dc-r7-brain-agent-invariants (2026-11-04, stream A Brain)

The pilot's agent turned a class-6 slip into six turns of 5 + 2 with cricket runs, and stayed off-topic until it gave up on maths. The hybrid plan says the LLM words the turn and code keeps the invariants, so these are code checks on her line, not prompt text. Reversal: if the full run shows the Director taking too many agent turns for false positives, loosen the tiny-sum rule first.

## dc-r7-brain-which-one (2026-11-04, stream A Brain)

She offered three choices, the child said yes, and she carried on with practice. That is the classic not-listening move. The choice stands until it is made.

## dc-r7-brain-game-screen-truth (2026-11-04, stream A Brain)

"Game ne 3 ko pehli side maana" describes a screen game that does not exist. Main thought it might be harness-only, but nothing stopped it in production either when no game was up. Screen truth applies to games too.
